newsitem.title: USA: Forecasts vary widely for US Jan payrolls data.
newsitem.headline: Forecasts vary widely for US Jan payrolls data.

text.p: Next Friday's report on U.S. employment is bound to give Treasury market participants the jitters, experts said.
They cited historical volatility in the Labor Department's January employment reports, stemming from seasonal factors, such as weather conditions and holiday hiring and sales.
And this January should be no exception to the trend.
The latest Reuters poll showed 20 experts are calling for payrolls to fall somewhere within a wide range of 150,000 to 400,000.
On average, they forecast 237,000 jobs were created in January, down from 262,000 new jobs in December, the poll showed.
Economists said U.S. Treasury market players will fixate on the payroll number despite the fact there is a broad range of possible outcomes.

"(Payrolls of) 270,000, 280,000 or 290,000 ... would be substantially structurally weaker -- because of seasonal factors -- than the 262,000 print we got a month ago," said Michael Strauss, senior vice president and chief economist at Sanwa Securities (USA) Co.
Strauss noted some experts refuse to rule out a jump in payrolls of some 400,000, adding that such an increase would be viewed unfavorably by the bond market.
"That would hurt us if we got 400,000, but if we get 400,000 in January, we'll get 100,000 in February. What helps in January, you lose in February," he added.

Market experts said the danger zone for the bond market would be a payroll number between 300,000 and 400,000, with the neutral zone 180,000 to 250,000 and a constructive range between 100,000 to 175,000.
However, the percent change in wages will play a crucial roll in the bond market's reaction to the headline payrolls figure, some economists said.

Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc, said the wage number is important, because "if we were to get a flat wage number even with a 300,000 employment, there may be relief in the market."
On the other hand, he said, "if we get a half-percent increase in the wages again, watch out -- especially if it is combined with a 300,000 employment number."
